subjects.name: Novel
subjects.intro: Longer fiction still in the public domain: social worlds, moral arguments, and plots that have outlasted their first printers. Each card below is a catalog entry, not a file stored here.

subjects.name: Romance
subjects.intro: Courtship, attachment, and the practical choices around them. These are older novels of feeling and manners, gathered as literature rather than as a modern romance shelf.

subjects.name: Mystery
subjects.intro: Cases, clues, and the pleasure of a pattern clicking shut. The Holmes books here are the early ones, long out of copyright, and the links leave this site for Open Library.

subjects.name: Gothic
subjects.intro: Dread, old houses, and the uncanny, in the literary sense. Covers, when Open Library has them, are loaded from their cover service. Nothing gothic is stored on this host.

subjects.name: Adventure
subjects.intro: Ships, roads, wilderness, and risk. These stories were written for a wide readership and remain in the public domain. Reading happens on Open Library, not on this catalog.

subjects.name: Children's books
subjects.intro: Tales long passed to young readers: Wonderland, Oz, the Secret Garden, and their shelf-mates. The catalog itself is written for a general audience looking up a public-domain text.

subjects.name: Science fiction
subjects.intro: Early speculative fiction about time, invention, and other worlds. Wells and Shelley sit here because the ideas travel, not because the editions are modern.

subjects.name: Short stories
subjects.intro: Tales and collections you can finish in a sitting, from Dubliners to a single strange story like The Yellow Wallpaper. Each entry links onward; this site does not keep the text.

subjects.name: Philosophy
subjects.intro: Meditations, essays, and arguments about how to live and how power behaves. Translations, where the original is not English, are older public-domain English versions named on the book page when we know them.

subjects.name: Memoir
subjects.intro: Lives told in the first person, kept as literature and as history. Douglass, Du Bois, and Thoreau are here because their books are public domain, and because a catalog should say whose voice you are opening.

authors.name: Jane Austen
authors.intro: Austen wrote six finished novels about money, rank, and judgment in English gentry life. The wit is social rather than sentimental: people reveal themselves by what they notice.

authors.name: Charlotte Brontë
authors.intro: Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre is a first-person account of work, conscience, and desire that refuses to treat the heroine as scenery. It remains one of the clearest voices in the nineteenth-century novel.

authors.name: Emily Brontë
authors.intro: Emily Brontë published one novel. Wuthering Heights is harsher than the love story its reputation sometimes suggests: a study of obsession set on a Yorkshire estate.

authors.name: Mary Shelley
authors.intro: Shelley wrote Frankenstein as a young novelist already thinking about responsibility, creation, and the stories the powerful tell about their mistakes. It is as much a moral tale as a tale of terror.

authors.name: Bram Stoker
authors.intro: Stoker’s Dracula is told through letters, diaries, and logs. The form matters: dread arrives as paperwork, travel notes, and the slow agreement that something impossible is true.

authors.name: Oscar Wilde
authors.intro: Wilde’s novel about Dorian Gray is a fable of vanity and influence, written with the same relish for sentences that marks his plays. The portrait changes so the man, for a while, does not.

authors.name: Arthur Conan Doyle
authors.intro: Doyle’s Sherlock Holmes stories invented a lasting shape for the detective tale: a client at the door, a clue others step over, and a companion who writes it down.

authors.name: Lewis Carroll
authors.intro: Carroll, the pen name of Charles Dodgson, sent Alice through a world that keeps changing the rules. The jokes are logical as often as they are whimsical.

authors.name: L. Frank Baum
authors.intro: Baum wanted American fairy tales that did not rely on the old European punishments. The Wonderful Wizard of Oz is the one that stuck: a road, a city, and a man behind a curtain.

authors.name: J. M. Barrie
authors.intro: Barrie’s Peter and Wendy is the novel of the boy who will not grow up. It is stranger and sadder than the later stage tradition sometimes allows.

authors.name: Robert Louis Stevenson
authors.intro: Stevenson could write a straight adventure and a nightmare about a divided self in the same decade. Treasure Island and Jekyll and Hyde are both exact about consequence.

authors.name: Charles Dickens
authors.intro: Dickens filled novels with institutions, comic speech, and people the city would rather not count. The books here run from a short Christmas tale to the long arc of Great Expectations.

authors.name: Herman Melville
authors.intro: Melville’s Moby-Dick begins as a whaling voyage and becomes a meditation on obsession, work, and what cannot be charted. The narrative voice never sits still for long.

authors.name: Mark Twain
authors.intro: Twain’s river books look like boyhood adventures and keep turning into arguments about conscience, fraud, and American speech. Huckleberry Finn is the one that refuses a tidy moral.

authors.name: Louisa May Alcott
authors.intro: Alcott’s Little Women follows four sisters through work, ambition, and domestic life without treating those subjects as small. It has been read as a family story and as a book about becoming a writer.

authors.name: L. M. Montgomery
authors.intro: Montgomery’s Anne Shirley talks her way into a Prince Edward Island household and then into a long series. The first book is the one in this catalog: a portrait of imagination under other people’s rules.

authors.name: Frances Hodgson Burnett
authors.intro: Burnett’s The Secret Garden is about a sour child, a locked garden, and the slow work of paying attention. The magic, such as it is, looks a great deal like care.

authors.name: Jack London
authors.intro: London’s Northland books put animals and people under the same pressure: cold, hunger, and the stories civilization tells about both. The Call of the Wild follows a dog out of California and into that pressure.

authors.name: H. G. Wells
authors.intro: Wells used impossible machines to write about class, empire, and the future as a place we might not like. The Time Machine and The War of the Worlds are the pair on this shelf.

authors.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
authors.intro: Gilman wrote The Yellow Wallpaper after a physician prescribed her a rest that forbade work. The story is short, domestic, and relentless about what that kind of care does to a mind.

authors.name: Kate Chopin
authors.intro: Chopin’s The Awakening follows Edna Pontellier as she steps out of a marriage the novel refuses to treat as her whole life. The ending is still argued over because the book does not soften it.

authors.name: Joseph Conrad
authors.intro: Conrad, who came to English as an adult, wrote Heart of Darkness as a framed tale about empire and the stories men tell when they come home. The narration is as much the subject as the journey.

authors.name: Franz Kafka
authors.intro: Kafka’s The Metamorphosis turns a traveling salesman into an insect and then watches the household reorganize around that fact. This catalog links a public-domain English translation, not a later one.

authors.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
authors.intro: Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment follows a student who tries to justify a murder and then has to live inside the justification. The English text linked here is an older public-domain translation.

authors.name: Leo Tolstoy
authors.intro: Tolstoy’s Anna Karenina sets a private catastrophe beside the ordinary work of a large social world. The catalog points to a public-domain English translation of the novel.

authors.name: Alexandre Dumas
authors.intro: Dumas built The Count of Monte Cristo on wrongful imprisonment, patience, and a fortune used as a plot. It is a long entertainment that keeps its eye on revenge as a life’s work.

authors.name: Victor Hugo
authors.intro: Hugo’s Les Misérables is a novel about a convict, a pursuit, and a city, with essays set into the story on purpose. The English version in this catalog is a public-domain translation.

authors.name: Miguel de Cervantes
authors.intro: Cervantes sent Don Quixote out to live by the rules of books he had read too well. The result is a comedy about reading itself. The link here is to a public-domain English translation.

authors.name: Homer
authors.intro: The Odyssey comes down under Homer’s name: a voyage home told in episodes of cunning, hospitality, and delay. This catalog uses Samuel Butler’s public-domain English prose translation.

authors.name: Marcus Aurelius
authors.intro: The Meditations are private notes by a Roman emperor, not a system written for pupils. They return, again and again, to what is and is not in a person’s control.

authors.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
authors.intro: Machiavelli’s The Prince is a short, blunt book about getting and keeping power. It has been read as advice, as satire, and as a report on how states actually behave.

authors.name: Henry David Thoreau
authors.intro: Thoreau’s Walden is the record of a stay in the woods and an argument about how much a life needs. The pond is real; the book is also a piece of rhetoric.

authors.name: Frederick Douglass
authors.intro: Douglass’s Narrative is an autobiography of enslavement and escape, written to make Northern readers unable to treat the facts as rumor. The voice is controlled, and the argument is public.

authors.name: W. E. B. Du Bois
authors.intro: Du Bois’s The Souls of Black Folk mixes essay, memoir, and music to describe life behind what he called the veil. It is a founding book of American letters, not only of sociology.

authors.name: Nathaniel Hawthorne
authors.intro: Hawthorne’s The Scarlet Letter sets a public punishment in a Puritan town and then studies the private lives around it. Guilt, in this novel, is as much a community habit as a feeling.

authors.name: James Joyce
authors.intro: Joyce’s Dubliners is a book of short stories about a city and the moments people fail to leave it. The collection is the public-domain Joyce on this shelf.

authors.name: F. Scott Fitzgerald
authors.intro: Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby is a short novel about money, invention, and a narrator who wants the party to mean something. It entered the public domain in the United States in 2021.

books.title: Pride and Prejudice
books.author: jane-austen
books.blurb: Elizabeth Bennet and Mr. Darcy misjudge each other in a comedy of marriage, income, and pride. Austen’s second published novel is still the surest entrance to her shelf.

books.title: Emma
books.author: jane-austen
books.blurb: Emma Woodhouse has money, leisure, and a talent for arranging other people’s lives. The novel lets her be charming and wrong in the same sentence.

books.title: Sense and Sensibility
books.author: jane-austen
books.blurb: Two sisters, turned out of their home, try sense and feeling as ways of surviving love and reduced means. It was Austen’s first published novel.

books.title: Persuasion
books.author: jane-austen
books.blurb: Anne Elliot broke an engagement years ago and has had to live quietly with the decision. A return of the man she refused gives the book its second chance.

books.title: Jane Eyre
books.author: charlotte-bronte
books.blurb: An orphan becomes a governess and refuses every arrangement that would make her less than a person. The house at Thornfield holds a secret the marriage plot cannot step around.

books.title: Wuthering Heights
books.author: emily-bronte
books.blurb: Heathcliff and Catherine’s attachment wrecks two households across two generations. The story is told by a tenant and a housekeeper, never by the pair at its center.

books.title: Frankenstein
books.author: mary-shelley
books.blurb: Victor Frankenstein builds a living being and then abandons it. The creature’s education, and Victor’s refusal to answer for what he made, are the book’s real experiment.

books.title: Dracula
books.author: bram-stoker
books.blurb: Jonathan Harker’s travel diary opens onto a count who intends to move to London. The rest of the novel is a coalition of notes, blood, and timetables trying to stop him.

books.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
books.author: oscar-wilde
books.blurb: A young man wishes that a portrait would age in his place. Wilde’s only novel follows the wish into influence, cruelty, and a picture locked in a room.

books.title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
books.author: arthur-conan-doyle
books.blurb: Twelve early cases, from a speckled band to a scandal in Bohemia, narrated by Dr. Watson. This is the collection that fixed Holmes in the popular imagination.

books.title: The Hound of the Baskervilles
books.author: arthur-conan-doyle
books.blurb: A family legend about a hound on the Devon moor brings Holmes out of a silence Doyle had meant to be permanent. The rational explanation has to earn its place against the fog.

books.title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
books.author: lewis-carroll
books.blurb: Alice follows a rabbit and finds a world that argues with her about size, manners, and the meaning of words. Carroll wrote it for a real child and then built a classic out of the joke.

books.title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
books.author: l-frank-baum
books.blurb: A cyclone carries Dorothy from Kansas to a road of yellow brick. The companions she picks up all want something a wizard in a city claims he can grant.

books.title: Peter and Wendy
books.author: j-m-barrie
books.blurb: The Darling children leave the nursery for Neverland with a boy who refuses the future. Barrie’s novel keeps the flying, and also the cost of never coming home.

books.title: Treasure Island
books.author: robert-louis-stevenson
books.blurb: Jim Hawkins finds a map and goes to sea with a crew that is not what the advertisement promised. Long John Silver remains the model of a charming villain.

books.title: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
books.author: robert-louis-stevenson
books.blurb: A London lawyer tries to understand the tie between a respectable doctor and a violent man who shares his house. Stevenson’s short novel is a study of a self split on purpose.

books.title: A Christmas Carol
books.author: charles-dickens
books.blurb: Ebenezer Scrooge is walked through his past, the present he refuses to see, and a future he can still change. Dickens wrote it quickly, and it became the Christmas story people mean.

books.title: A Tale of Two Cities
books.author: charles-dickens
books.blurb: London and Paris before and during the French Revolution, joined by a look-alike, a prisoner, and a sacrifice. The opening sentence is famous; the plot earns it.

books.title: Great Expectations
books.author: charles-dickens
books.blurb: Pip is lifted out of a forge by money whose source he misunderstands. Dickens’s late novel is about class, gratitude, and the patron Pip invents in his head.

books.title: Moby-Dick
books.author: herman-melville
books.blurb: Ishmael ships on the Pequod under a captain hunting one white whale. The book stops for whales, work, and metaphysics, then returns to the chase.

books.title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
books.author: mark-twain
books.blurb: Huck Finn fakes his death and rafts the Mississippi with Jim, who is escaping enslavement. Twain’s novel is funny, and it does not let the joke forgive the country it travels.

books.title: Little Women
books.author: louisa-may-alcott
books.blurb: Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy March grow up in a household short of money and long on opinions. Jo’s wish to write is as much the plot as any marriage.

books.title: Anne of Green Gables
books.author: l-m-montgomery
books.blurb: Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert ask for a boy from the orphanage and receive Anne Shirley. She talks, imagines, and slowly makes herself necessary to Avonlea.

books.title: The Secret Garden
books.author: frances-hodgson-burnett
books.blurb: Mary Lennox arrives at a Yorkshire manor and finds a garden no one is allowed to enter. Tending it changes her, and the cousin shut in another room.

books.title: The Call of the Wild
books.author: jack-london
books.blurb: Buck, a stolen California dog, is worked north into the Yukon. London tells the story from the animal’s side of the harness.

books.title: The Time Machine
books.author: h-g-wells
books.blurb: A Victorian inventor rides his machine to a future in which humanity has split. Wells’s novella is a social argument dressed as a traveler’s report.

books.title: The War of the Worlds
books.author: h-g-wells
books.blurb: Martian cylinders fall on the English countryside and the narrator walks through the collapse of ordinary life. Wells aimed the invasion at the empire that had invaded others.

books.title: The Yellow Wallpaper
books.author: charlotte-perkins-gilman
books.blurb: A woman confined to a room for her health begins to watch the pattern in the wallpaper. Gilman’s story is brief and does not offer the cure the physician promised.

books.title: The Awakening
books.author: kate-chopin
books.blurb: Edna Pontellier, a wife in Creole New Orleans, stops agreeing that her life is already decided. Chopin’s novel was received coldly and later read as a classic.

books.title: Heart of Darkness
books.author: joseph-conrad
books.blurb: Marlow tells a deck audience about his trip upriver to find Kurtz, an ivory agent who has become a rumor. Conrad’s tale is about empire and about storytelling.

books.title: The Metamorphosis
books.author: franz-kafka
books.blurb: Gregor Samsa wakes as an insect and worries first about missing the train. The household’s patience, and then its accounting, are the rest of the story. The link is to a public-domain English translation.

books.title: Crime and Punishment
books.author: fyodor-dostoevsky
books.blurb: Raskolnikov tests a theory that some people may kill for a higher purpose, and the theory does not survive the act. This entry points to a public-domain English translation.

books.title: Anna Karenina
books.author: leo-tolstoy
books.blurb: Anna’s affair and Levin’s search for a workable life run side by side in imperial Russia. Tolstoy gives the social world as much weight as the passion. The link is to a public-domain English translation.

books.title: The Count of Monte Cristo
books.author: alexandre-dumas
books.blurb: Edmond Dantès is imprisoned on a false charge and comes back, years later, with a new name and a plan. Dumas makes patience itself into an adventure.

books.title: Les Misérables
books.author: victor-hugo
books.blurb: Jean Valjean leaves prison and is pursued across France by Inspector Javert, while Hugo pauses to write about sewers, convents, and justice. The catalog links a public-domain English translation.

books.title: Don Quixote
books.author: miguel-de-cervantes
books.blurb: A country gentleman renames himself a knight and rides out to enforce the plots of chivalric books. Cervantes’s novel is the comedy of taking reading literally. The link is to a public-domain English translation.

books.title: The Odyssey
books.author: homer
books.blurb: After the war at Troy, Odysseus tries to get home while suitors occupy his house. This catalog links Samuel Butler’s public-domain prose translation, not a modern verse one.

books.title: Meditations
books.author: marcus-aurelius
books.blurb: Private notes on judgment, death, and the discipline of wanting less than circumstances offer. The English text here is a public-domain translation of the emperor’s Greek.

books.title: The Prince
books.author: niccolo-machiavelli
books.blurb: A short treatise on acquiring and holding a state, written in exile and dedicated to a Medici. Machiavelli prefers what rulers do to what mirror-books said they should do.

books.title: Walden
books.author: henry-david-thoreau
books.blurb: Thoreau’s account of two years in a cabin by Walden Pond, arranged by season and by argument. It is a book about economy in the old sense: how a life is furnished.

books.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
books.author: frederick-douglass
books.blurb: Douglass describes enslavement in Maryland, the fight to read, and his escape. He published the Narrative to answer readers who claimed no one in bondage could have written it.

books.title: The Souls of Black Folk
books.author: w-e-b-du-bois
books.blurb: Essays on reconstruction, education, music, and what Du Bois named double consciousness. The book argues, and it also remembers.

books.title: The Scarlet Letter
books.author: nathaniel-hawthorne
books.blurb: Hester Prynne wears a letter the town requires, while the father of her child stays unnamed. Hawthorne’s novel is about punishment as a public art.

books.title: Dubliners
books.author: james-joyce
books.blurb: Fifteen stories of Dublin life, ending with The Dead. Joyce called the method a kind of clarity; the characters often stop just short of changing.

books.title: The Great Gatsby
books.author: f-scott-fitzgerald
books.blurb: Nick Carraway rents a house next to Jay Gatsby’s parties and slowly learns what the parties are for. Fitzgerald’s novel entered the public domain in the United States in 2021.
